strengths: Novel, well-motivated dataset addressing a real problem in multilingual government websites; first document-level cross-lingual RSD benchmark with human annotations

Comprehensive evaluation across diverse model types (unsupervised, few-shot LLMs, fine-tuned LLMs, encoders) revealing substantial performance gaps (up to 78-point Spearman drop) between synthetic and naturalistic data
Clear, impactful findings: demonstrates LLM failures on long documents, formatting errors, underlabeling; shows unsupervised DiffAlign surprisingly robust
Rigorous dataset construction with detailed guidelines, trial phase feedback, interactive annotation interface, and systematic quality control filtering
Excellent reproducibility with released code/data and comprehensive documentation (appendices, prompts, implementation details); honest discussion of limitations
weaknesses: Significant annotation quality concerns: inconsistent inter-annotator agreement across language pairs (EN-DE IoU 11.17% vs EN-IT 32.10%), only 2 annotators, only 25 of 224 documents overlap-validated, subjective annotation strategies documented but unresolved (whole phrase vs minimal labeling, omission handling divergence)

Limited generalizability: only high-resource, closely-related European languages with Latin scripts and English-centric pairs; government domain specificity; unclear transfer to other languages, scripts, or domains

Experimental design weaknesses: (1) unequal training data (LLMs 560 augmentations vs encoders 10,000), (2) asymmetric LLM evaluation on SwissGov due to computational constraints, (3) no specified train/test split for the main SwissGov-RSD dataset, (4) label projection validated on only 50 samples with 34-46% sample-level edits
No methodological novelty: applies existing techniques (DiffAlign, LLM prompting, standard fine-tuning); contribution primarily dataset-focused without algorithmic advances

Dataset size modest for modern standards (224 documents); sparse overlap annotation assessment (25 pairs); unresolved questions about EN-DE vs EN-IT agreement gap (3× difference); moderate label correlations especially for EN-DE (66.16% for fuzzy ≥50%)

strengths: Addresses practical real-world problem with compelling motivating examples (multilingual government content alignment)
Naturalistic dataset with real semantic differences, addressing limitations of synthetic iSTS-RSD benchmark
Comprehensive benchmarking of 25+ approaches (unsupervised, few-shot LLMs, fine-tuned LLMs, encoders)
Important empirical finding: substantial performance gap (up to 78 Spearman correlation points) between synthetic and realistic settings
Meticulous documentation of annotation process with detailed guidelines, inter-annotator agreement metrics, and transparent methodology
Strong reproducibility: code/data promised for release, complete implementation details and hyperparameters provided
Systematic evaluation revealing specific failure modes (LLM output format errors, document length sensitivity, underlabeling toward document ends)
weaknesses: Inter-annotator agreement is modest (Spearman 43.61–65.09; mean IoU 23.98–32.10), raising concerns about gold standard quality for a token-level task
Severely limited scope: only 3 closely-related European languages, Latin scripts, English-centric pairs, government domain; generalizability to other languages and domains unclear
Dataset size modest (~186K tokens per language pair, 224 documents total); small for modern deep learning and limited to two annotators per pair
Task formulation under-specified: cross-lingual token alignment procedure not clearly described; handling of tokenization differences across languages not discussed
Extremely low overall performance (best Spearman ~6–7 on SwissGov-RSD) limits insights into solvability; no human performance baseline for reference
No novel methodological contributions: paper benchmarks existing approaches without proposing methods tailored to document-level cross-lingual RSD
Limited error analysis: no systematic study of challenging linguistic phenomena, error types by model, or linguistic drivers of semantic differences
Label projection introduces potential biases: only 50 samples per language pair manually verified; impact on model performance not studied
Evaluation metric not justified: Spearman correlation assumes ordered scale, but semantic differences may be categorical; alternative metrics not explored
LLM prompting not optimized: simple uniform prompts acknowledged as limiting, but sophisticated strategies (example selection, iterative refinement) not explored
